Lecture 7

Lattices, centres and global forms

What this lecture does

The groups SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) and SO⁡(3)\SO(3)SO(3) have isomorphic Lie algebras but are not isomorphic. This lecture asks which discrete data determine connected groups with the same Lie algebra. For compact groups, the answer is the kernel lattice Λ\LambdaΛ of a maximal torus, inside its Lie algebra t\algtt, read together with the root data.

The lecture proves this for semisimple Lie algebras, using cited structure results. Different lattices can still give isomorphic groups, through automorphisms of the Lie algebra that preserve t\algtt. When there is a central torus, the lecture shows how Λ\LambdaΛ determines a finite group FFF.

The Lie groups denoted KKK or TTT in this lecture, with or without subscripts, are connected. The subgroups CCC, FFF and Z(K)Z(K)Z(K) that appear later need not be connected. A Lie group and its identity component have the same Lie algebra, so we restrict to connected groups. Even connected groups with isomorphic Lie algebras need not be isomorphic, as SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) and SO⁡(3)\SO(3)SO(3) show.

7.1 Compact connected abelian groups

Definition 7.1. A torus is a Lie group isomorphic to U⁡(1)n\UU(1)^nU(1)n for some n≥0n\ge0n≥0. A lattice in a real vector space VVV is a subgroup Zv1⊕⋯⊕Zvn\mathbb{Z}v_1\oplus\dots\oplus\mathbb{Z}v_nZv1​⊕⋯⊕Zvn​, where v1,…,vnv_1,\dots,v_nv1​,…,vn​ is a basis of VVV.

Lemma 7.2 (Discrete subgroups). Every discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real vector space equals Zv1⊕⋯⊕Zvk\mathbb{Z}v_1\oplus\dots\oplus\mathbb{Z}v_kZv1​⊕⋯⊕Zvk​ for some linearly independent v1,…,vkv_1,\dots,v_kv1​,…,vk​.

We cite this standard lemma from BD, Section I.3, Lemma (3.8).

Theorem 7.3. Let TTT be a compact connected abelian Lie group with Lie algebra t\algtt of dimension nnn. Then exp⁡ ⁣:t→T\exp\colon\algt\to Texp:t→T is a surjective homomorphism, and Λ=ker⁡exp⁡\Lambda=\ker\expΛ=kerexp is a lattice in t\algtt. For a basis v1,…,vnv_1,\dots,v_nv1​,…,vn​ of Λ\LambdaΛ, the map Φ ⁣:U⁡(1)n→T,Φ(e2πix1,…,e2πixn)=exp⁡(x1v1+⋯+xnvn),\Phi\colon\UU(1)^n\to T,\qquad \Phi\bigl(e^{2\pi ix_1},\dots,e^{2\pi ix_n}\bigr)=\exp(x_1v_1+\dots+x_nv_n),Φ:U(1)n→T,Φ(e2πix1​,…,e2πixn​)=exp(x1​v1​+⋯+xn​vn​), is an isomorphism of Lie groups.

If H,H′∈ΛH,H'\in\LambdaH,H′∈Λ and H′∈H+UH'\in H+UH′∈H+U, then H′−H∈Λ∩UH'-H\in\Lambda\cap UH′−H∈Λ∩U, so H′=HH'=HH′=H. Hence Λ\LambdaΛ is discrete. Isomorphism. Changing xjx_jxj​ by an integer changes ∑jxjvj\sum_jx_jv_j∑j​xj​vj​ by an element of Λ\LambdaΛ. So Φ\PhiΦ is a well-defined homomorphism. It is continuous, because near any point it is the composite of a local inverse of x↦(e2πixj)jx\mapsto(e^{2\pi ix_j})_jx↦(e2πixj​)j​ with the continuous map x↦exp⁡(∑jxjvj)x\mapsto\exp(\sum_jx_jv_j)x↦exp(∑j​xj​vj​). It is bijective because ker⁡exp⁡=⨁jZvj\ker\exp=\bigoplus_j\mathbb{Z}v_jkerexp=⨁j​Zvj​. A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism. Lecture 6 defined a torus as a compact connected abelian Lie group. The theorem shows that such a group is a torus in the sense above, and the converse is clear. So the two definitions agree. The theorem also proves the statement T≅t/ΛT\cong\algt/\LambdaT≅t/Λ cited in Lecture 6, and it uses nothing from that lecture.

7.2 Characters and cocharacters

Definition 7.4. A character of a torus TTT is a continuous homomorphism χ ⁣:T→U⁡(1)\chi\colon T\to\UU(1)χ:T→U(1). A cocharacter is a continuous homomorphism λ ⁣:U⁡(1)→T\lambda\colon\UU(1)\to Tλ:U(1)→T. Under pointwise multiplication, the characters form a group X∗(T)X^*(T)X∗(T) and the cocharacters form a group X∗(T)X_*(T)X∗​(T).

These characters are one-dimensional. Trace characters return in Lecture 9.

Theorem 7.9 (Centre). Let KKK be compact connected with maximal torus TTT. Then Z(K)⊂TZ(K)\subset TZ(K)⊂T, and exp⁡\expexp restricts to a surjective homomorphism P∨→Z(K)P^\vee\to Z(K)P∨→Z(K) with kernel Λ\LambdaΛ. Thus Z(K)≅P∨/ΛZ(K)\cong P^\vee/\LambdaZ(K)≅P∨/Λ.

Proof. Let z∈Z(K)z\in Z(K)z∈Z(K). By Lecture 6, z=gtg−1z=gtg^{-1}z=gtg−1 for some g∈Kg\in Kg∈K and t∈Tt\in Tt∈T. Since zzz is central, t=g−1zg=zt=g^{-1}zg=zt=g−1zg=z, so z∈Tz\in Tz∈T.

Next we show that g∈Kg\in Kg∈K is central if and only if Ad⁡(g)=id⁡\Ad(g)=\idAd(g)=id. If ggg is central, differentiating gexp⁡(sX)g−1=exp⁡(sX)g\exp(sX)g^{-1}=\exp(sX)gexp(sX)g−1=exp(sX) at s=0s=0s=0 gives Ad⁡(g)=id⁡\Ad(g)=\idAd(g)=id. If Ad⁡(g)=id⁡\Ad(g)=\idAd(g)=id, then gexp⁡(X)g−1=exp⁡(Ad⁡(g)X)=exp⁡Xg\exp(X)g^{-1}=\exp(\Ad(g)X)=\exp Xgexp(X)g−1=exp(Ad(g)X)=expX. The elements exp⁡X\exp XexpX generate the connected group KKK (Lecture 2), so ggg is central.

Now write z=exp⁡Hz=\exp Hz=expH with H∈tH\in\algtH∈t, using the surjectivity of exp⁡\expexp in the torus classification, Theorem 7.3. The operator Ad⁡(exp⁡H)=ead⁡H\Ad(\exp H)=e^{\ad H}Ad(expH)=eadH is the identity on tC\algt_\CtC​ and multiplication by eiα(H)e^{i\alpha(H)}eiα(H) on gα\g_\alphagα​. Hence, by the criterion just proved, exp⁡H\exp HexpH is central exactly when H∈P∨H\in P^\veeH∈P∨. The kernel of exp⁡\expexp on P∨P^\veeP∨ is Λ∩P∨=Λ\Lambda\cap P^\vee=\LambdaΛ∩P∨=Λ. 

For the fundamental group we cite the following theorem.

Theorem 7.10 (Fundamental group; H, Chapter 13; BD, Section V.7). Let KKK be a compact connected Lie group with maximal torus TTT. Then π1(K)≅Λ/Q∨=X∗(T)/Q∨.\pi_1(K)\cong\Lambda/Q^\vee=X_*(T)/Q^\vee.π1​(K)≅Λ/Q∨=X∗​(T)/Q∨.

Call KKK semisimple if k\algkk is semisimple. Then RRR spans t∗\algt^*t∗, and the simple roots form a basis of t∗\algt^*t∗. The simple coroots form a basis of t\algtt (the Lie Algebras course, via hα=−iHαh_\alpha=-iH_\alphahα​=−iHα​). So all four subgroups are lattices, and the inclusions above have finite index. Weyl’s theorem states that a compact connected semisimple group has finite fundamental group and compact universal cover (H, Chapter 13; Knapp, Chapter IV).

Groups with a central torus

In U⁡(2)\UU(2)U(2) the element −I-I−I is both a scalar and an element of SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2). A representation must act on it consistently. Exercise 4.3 did this by hand. We now state the condition for a general central torus.

If k\algkk has nonzero centre, then Z(K)Z(K)Z(K) is infinite and RRR does not span t∗\algt^*t∗. Moreover, P∨P^\veeP∨ contains the centre of k\algkk, so P∨P^\veeP∨ is not a lattice. The proposition on forms of a semisimple algebra, Proposition 7.11, does not apply. We use a structure theorem instead.

We recall the global structure theorem of Lecture 6, together with the splitting of that lecture.

Theorem 7.14 (Global structure; recalled from Lecture 6; BD, Section V.8; Knapp, Chapter IV). Let KKK be compact connected. Let T0T_0T0​ be the identity component of Z(K)Z(K)Z(K), with Lie algebra t0\algt_0t0​. Let KscK_{sc}Ksc​ be the simply connected group with Lie algebra [k,k][\algk,\algk][k,k]. Thus K≅(T0×Ksc)/FK\cong(T_0\times K_{sc})/FK≅(T0​×Ksc​)/F.

Proposition 7.15. In the global structure theorem, Theorem 7.14, let TscT_{sc}Tsc​ be a maximal torus of KscK_{sc}Ksc​ with Lie algebra tsc\algt_{sc}tsc​, and let TTT be the image of T0×TscT_0\times T_{sc}T0​×Tsc​. Each root space satisfies gα=[t,gα]⊂[k,k]C\g_\alpha=[\algt,\g_\alpha]\subset[\algk,\algk]_\Cgα​=[t,gα​]⊂[k,k]C​. Summary

A compact connected abelian Lie group is t/Λ\algt/\Lambdat/Λ, and its characters are the ℓ\ellℓ with ℓ(Λ)⊂2πZ\ell(\Lambda)\subset2\pi\mathbb{Z}ℓ(Λ)⊂2πZ. For compact connected KKK, the kernel lattice satisfies Q∨⊂Λ⊂P∨Q^\vee\subset\Lambda\subset P^\veeQ∨⊂Λ⊂P∨. The kernel lattice gives Z(K)≅P∨/ΛZ(K)\cong P^\vee/\LambdaZ(K)≅P∨/Λ and, by a cited theorem, π1(K)≅Λ/Q∨\pi_1(K)\cong\Lambda/Q^\veeπ1​(K)≅Λ/Q∨.

For semisimple k\algkk, the connected forms correspond to lattices between Q∨Q^\veeQ∨ and P∨P^\veeP∨. Lattices related by an automorphism of k\algkk preserving t\algtt give isomorphic groups. With a central torus, write K≅(T0×Ksc)/FK\cong(T_0\times K_{sc})/FK≅(T0​×Ksc​)/F, where F≅Λ/(Λ0⊕Q∨)F\cong\Lambda/(\Lambda_0\oplus Q^\vee)F≅Λ/(Λ0​⊕Q∨). A pair (ℓ0,ℓ)(\ell_0,\ell)(ℓ0​,ℓ) is then a character of the maximal torus exactly when ℓ0(Λ0)⊂2πZ\ell_0(\Lambda_0)\subset2\pi\mathbb{Z}ℓ0​(Λ0​)⊂2πZ, ℓ∈Psc\ell\in P_{sc}ℓ∈Psc​, and the product is trivial on FFF.

Lecture 8 uses X∗(T)X^*(T)X∗(T) to state the classification of representations by highest weights.
